# University of Melbourne: Overview
The University of Melbourne, founded in 1853, is one of Australia’s leading research-intensive universities with its primary campus at Parkville and additional campuses at Burnley, Southbank, Werribee, Creswick, Dookie, Shepparton, and soon Fishermans Bend. The university is organized into nine faculties encompassing major disciplines such as Arts, Science, Medicine, Law, Engineering, Fine Arts, Business, Education, and Architecture. Its governance is overseen by a 13-member Council and an Academic Board, with the Vice-Chancellor and Chancellor leading its executive.
Melbourne consistently ranks as Australia's top university in aggregate global rankings (QS, THE, ARWU), attaining 19th (QS), 37th (THE), and 38th (ARWU) globally in 2026. The university is recognized for outstanding research output and citation impact, with expenditures second only to CSIRO and connections to over 100 research centers and institutes. International students make up 44% of the student body. Undergraduate admissions are highly selective, with the median ATAR at 94.05, and admission is supported by access pathways for underrepresented groups. The Melbourne Model, introduced in 2008, defines its academic structure, requiring a broad undergraduate degree before specialization at postgraduate level.

# Student Life and Notable Achievements
Student life at Melbourne is vibrant, featuring over 200 clubs through the Student Union and extensive graduate representation. The university’s residential colleges and halls foster community and academic engagement, while the university’s museums, galleries, and libraries support a rich academic culture. Melbourne University Sport oversees numerous clubs and sporting teams, some with historic standing such as the oldest lacrosse club globally and a prominent rowing club.
The university has produced notable alumni across fields, including multiple Prime Ministers of Australia (Julia Gillard, Robert Menzies, Alfred Deakin, Harold Holt), Nobel Laureates (Elizabeth Blackburn, Howard Florey, Frank Macfarlane Burnet, John Eccles, Richard Robson, Bert Sakmann, Joshua Lederberg, Sir James Mirrlees), and cultural figures like Cate Blanchett, Germaine Greer, Barry Humphries, and Peter Singer. The leadership includes a historic roster of Chancellors and Vice-Chancellors, with Emma Johnston appointed as the first woman Vice-Chancellor in 2024.
